body:
In a new research piece, multi-strategy manager Davidson Kempner Capital Management argues that hedge funds now offer the liquidity that private markets-heavy portfolios will need.

The white paper, _When the Tide Turns: Absolute Return’s Liquidity Advantage_, concludes that investors may benefit from raising allocations to liquid absolute return and hedge fund strategies as a safeguard against market downturns.

The firm estimates that alternative assets have grown to $24 trillion globally, but 88% of those assets are now invested in illiquid or semi-liquid strategies, up from 74% in 2000.

“With the 10 largest stocks now accounting for 35% of the U.S. equity market — near-record concentration that heightens portfolio risk — and alternative investments becoming increasingly illiquid, we believe it is timely to examine the role that more liquid absolute return strategies can play in portfolios,” wrote Tony Yoseloff, managing partner and chief investment officer, and Suzanne Gibbons, partner and head of research.

Using a stress-test framework based on the Federal Reserve’s 2026 severely adverse scenario, the firm modeled several endowment-style portfolios with varying levels of liquidity. It found that portfolios with at least a 15% allocation to quarterly liquid hedge funds outperformed comparable portfolios invested in illiquid direct lending by 19% from market trough through recovery. Increasing the liquid hedge fund allocation to 25% and cutting private equity by 10 percentage points boosted the advantage to 24%, largely by allowing investors to avoid forced sales of equities at depressed valuations and to rebalance into risk assets during the recovery.

The paper highlights mounting pressures in private markets, including historically low private equity distributions since 2022, growing concentrations of aging portfolio holdings and redemption strains among semi-liquid private credit vehicles. Davidson Kempner contends that few studies have measured what illiquidity costs a whole portfolio during periods of market stress, particularly when capital calls rise and liquidity needs increase.

The firm, which manages more than $40 billion in assets, has for many years been a staple of institutional hedge fund portfolios. More recently, the four-decade-old firm has also expanded into private market investments, including credit and real estate strategies.

In a white paper earlier this year, Yoseloff and Gibbons highlighted the decline in the pace of private equity distributions and lower returns as a problem for allocators. Their proposed solution: the relatively small $640 billion opportunistic credit market.

Still, the team has stayed close to its multi-strategy roots, with decades of experience investing across relative value, merger arbitrage and event-driven strategies. Davidson Kempner generated $4.4 billion in net gains for investors in 2025 and $28.9 billion since inception, placing 18th in Edmond de Rothschild’s 20 Greatest Money Managers ranking.

In the new white paper, the team argues that hedge funds could serve as a more effective portfolio ballast than traditional fixed income. Davidson Kempner notes that stock-bond correlations turned positive in 2022, reducing bonds’ diversification benefits, while credit hedge funds generated approximately 260 basis points of additional annualized return compared with fixed-income benchmarks at similar levels of volatility from 2000 through September. The firm expects institutional investors to shift allocations away from private equity and direct lending in favor of more liquid hedge fund strategies as the value of liquidity becomes more apparent.

Hedge fund inflows have continued in November, with the SS&C GlobeOp Capital Movement Index advancing 0.52%.

Davidson Kempner also found that hedge funds have become less liquid over the years. The firm estimated that only 52% of hedge fund assets can be fully redeemed within a year, compared with 70% in 2000. It attributed the shift largely to heavier use of leverage, especially among large multi-managers.

Gross asset-weighted leverage at multi-strategy hedge funds, a group that includes multi-managers, more than doubled to 12x between the start of 2020 and the end of June, according to SEC Form PF data cited in the paper.

Seven large multi-managers tracked by PivotalPath averaged roughly 10x gross leverage, compared with less than 3x at more traditional multi-strategy funds. According to Davidson Kempner, more leverage means more risk from crowded positioning, because managers forced to deleverage at the same time may have to unwind similar trades together. At 10x leverage, a 5% decline in gross assets translates into a 50% loss of fund capital. To keep investor withdrawals from forcing that kind of unwind during a drawdown, multi-managers lock up capital for longer.

Davidson Kempner continues to call the 2020s the “decade of absolute return.” In a 2025 white paper, it showed that since 1990, absolute return strategies have averaged 52% higher excess returns during periods of elevated interest rates. Higher rates, the firm argues, help these strategies by separating winners from losers, which widens return dispersion and creates more room for alpha.
